surfaces.part: sign head (oval cap plate, white top with teal underside)

answer.evidence: The width profile of the head runs 6, 12, 14, 16, 16, 14, 16, 16, 14, 12, then drops to 8 for the shaft at row 10. It widens and then narrows again, so it is an ellipse-like plate that overhangs the shaft. Rows 1-6 are the bright top surface. Rows 7-9 are a darker teal band that works as the front edge and eave shadow. Below it, the 8-wide shaft (rows 10-21) carries the number plate, and the base flares out in rows 22-29. That gives a front face of about 20 rows.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a single-tile bollard-style sign: a pole with a round cap and a yellow number plate. It shows 11 visible tones per tile, close to kiosk-a (12), above bus-shelter-a (6) and below vending-a (20). Near-flat coverage is 0%, so there are no large flat fills. Dark edge pixels are 0% neutral, so the outline is tinted and reads as a dark version of the adjacent material, as in the references. The cap and post have about 4 lightness steps, one fewer than the references' 5, and the grey shaft has little grain or dither. Overall it is plausibly accepted next to the references, but it looks a little thinner and simpler than vending-a and kiosk-a. Because it is a thin single-tile prop, sparseness alone is not grounds for failure, but the modest shading depth and the small amount of texture are borderline. The measured facts support density comparable to the shipped modern_city art.

It overhangs the 8 px shaft by 4 px on each side, which reads as an elliptical cap plate. The shaft below (rows 10-29) is a front face with a number plate and a flared base. The cap is a somewhat blobby, cloud-like ellipse, so the top-surface evidence is plausible but not strong.
